claims.text: High configurational entropy coupled with local chemical fluctuations stabilizes a single- or dual-phase structure in multi-principal-element nanoalloys heated to 600–1200 °C under inert atmosphere.
Entropy and local chemical fluctuations reduce the driving force for phase segregation.
The proposed stabilization preserves both chemical homogeneity and grain size at elevated temperatures.
The starting powders are equiatomic or near-equiatomic, uniformly fine-grained, and contain minimal oxide.
Changing Al content from approximately 0.1 to 0.3 in a quinary nanoalloy will systematically vary the relevant stabilization behavior.
Compositional heterogeneity and entropic stabilization affect short-range order.
A B2 plus disordered-BCC mixture is an example of a stable two-phase state relevant to the proposed nanoalloys.
High configurational entropy lowers the free-energy difference between competing phases.
Variation in constituent atomic sizes decreases atomic diffusion.
Variation in constituent atomic sizes promotes local lattice distortion.
Entropy, reduced diffusion, and lattice distortion collectively suppress large-scale phase separation and grain growth at elevated temperature.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will show at least approximately twofold slower grain growth than a lower-entropy alloy of similar average composition.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will maintain a coherent or partially coherent phase assemblage throughout 600–1200 °C.
The lower-entropy baseline will undergo extensive phase separation and coarsening under the same thermal conditions.
The prediction is limited to near-equiatomic multi-principal-element nanoalloys with minimal volatile species, inert environments, and uniform fine-grained starting structures.
Phase changes may accelerate outside 600–1200 °C or in non-inert environments.
